governance.summary: The company decides. Residents are customers with a contract, so their say comes through feedback and surveys, and through the simple choice to stay or to leave when the terms stop suiting them.
governance.body: In operator coliving the company owns or leases the building and sets the rules. It decides who can move in and what the house rules are. It also decides how events are run and what the price will be. Residents sign an agreement, often for a few months to a year, and have little formal power over the building. Operators usually have a community manager who listens to requests and passes on complaints, and who organises activities. Some run surveys or resident committees that advise and do not decide. The clear rules and quick decisions suit people who want no meetings. The trade is that the operator's interests and the residents' interests can diverge, and when they do the operator sets the terms.

example.text: Habyt runs furnished coliving across Europe and Asia and sets the terms centrally for its many buildings.

governance.pitfall: Residents can lose their home through a change in policy or price, with no vote on it.

financing.summary: Investors fund the buildings. The monthly rent covers the room and the shared spaces, along with the services. Residents own nothing and pay one price.
financing.body: Operator coliving is a business funded by investors, who put money into leasing or building properties and fitting them out. The operator earns it back through rent. The monthly price usually includes the furnished room and the utilities. Internet and cleaning are covered too, along with access to the shared areas, which is where the convenience comes from. Compared with a normal rental the price is often higher, and the lease is short and flexible. Operators grow quickly with outside money, and that makes them exposed to shifts in demand and rents, and to the cost of credit. Some work on management contracts for property owners and some run their own buildings. Residents have no equity and no stake in how the money is used.

example.text: The Collective opened a huge London scheme in 2016, and its operating company went into administration five years later.

financing.pitfall: A company that expands faster than demand can fail, and residents lose the community they paid for.

space.summary: A private furnished room that is often small sits beside shared kitchens and lounges designed by the company. The quality is polished and consistent from one building to the next.
space.body: Spaces are designed as a product. A resident gets a furnished private room, sometimes with its own bathroom, and access to shared kitchens and lounges. Many buildings add workspaces and a gym or terrace. The design is professional and uses hotel-style finishes, with the same look across buildings. Rooms tend to be compact, which pushes people into the shared areas. Some buildings are purpose-built, such as student blocks. Others are converted offices or hotels, or older apartment houses. Rooms are standardised so they can be rented and cleaned quickly. The result is clean and ready to use on the first day. Residents have little room to change anything, so the place can feel more like a hotel than a home.

example.text: Campus1 MTL is purpose-built student coliving in downtown Montréal.

space.pitfall: Beautiful shared spaces can still feel empty if nobody uses them.

community.summary: The operator plans the events and tries to match residents. Friendships do form, often through the daily overlap, and sometimes in spite of the planning.
community.body: Community is delivered as a service. The operator hires a community manager and runs weekly dinners or workshops. It sometimes screens applicants so the mix feels right. The calendar is full of activities and the app helps residents find each other. For someone new to a city, this gives a quick social start with no effort. Because attendance is voluntary and residents come and go, the community changes often. The bonds are lighter than in a self-built group. Real friendships tend to grow out of the shared kitchen and the late conversations, more than out of the scheduled event. Operators that cut costs often cut the community role first, and the social life fades with it.

example.text: Cohabs runs coliving house by house in Brussels and Paris as well as New York, with a host for each location.

community.pitfall: Community that is bought can disappear when the budget for events or staff is cut.

operations.summary: This is where operators are strongest. Staff and an app handle the cleaning and the repairs. They also handle bills and bookings, so residents do very little themselves.
operations.body: Operators run buildings as a service. Staff clean the shared areas and fix problems. They manage the move-in and move-out. They also handle bills and contracts. An app often covers bookings and payments. Maintenance requests and event sign-ups go through it as well. Residents do not share chores or negotiate who does the dishes in the same way. A single monthly price covers all of it. This professional running is a main reason people choose operator coliving, and it is usually reliable. It is also where costs sit. The staff and the software have to be paid for by rent, along with the cleaning. When margins get thin the services shrink first, and residents notice quickly. Rent pays for all of this, so the standard of service depends on the operator staying profitable.

example.text: Habyt grew by taking over other operators such as Common. It runs the buildings through a single platform.

operations.pitfall: When margins tighten the cleaning and the support get cut before anything else.

privacy.summary: A private room with a lock, and shared areas you can use or skip. Rules are set by contract, and disputes go to the operator.
privacy.body: Privacy is similar to a good shared flat or a hotel. Residents have a lockable room, and most of the building is shared. Staff may enter for cleaning or repairs under notice, and the operator sets rules for guests and for noise, as well as for use of common areas. Conflicts between residents go first to the community manager, who can talk to those involved or move someone to another room. For serious breaches, the operator can end a contract, and the resident has little ground to contest it beyond what the agreement and local tenant law say. This is simple and quick, and it offers no neutral third party. Some people like the distance this gives them from neighbours.

example.text: The Collective offered private studios alongside large shared lounges and kitchens in its London building.

privacy.pitfall: A dispute with the operator has no neutral place to go beyond the contract and the courts.

leaving.summary: Leaving is easy. You give notice and pack a bag, and there is no equity to sell. The cost is that nothing you build there is yours.
leaving.body: Contracts are designed to be flexible. Residents often sign for a few months to a year and can leave with a short notice period. The furniture stays behind, and so do the internet and the cleaning, so a move is light. There is no purchase and no resale, and no share to recover beyond a deposit. This makes operator coliving good for transitions, such as a new job or a semester, or a move to a new city. It does not offer long-term security. Rents can rise and buildings can be sold or closed, which has left residents looking for new homes at short notice. Most are not designed for growing old, since the model targets young adults and students.

example.text: When The Collective's operator failed, its London building was left to be sold and run by others.

leaving.pitfall: A building can be sold or closed, and residents may have little time to find another home.

whoPoints: People new to a city who want a furnished room and an instant social layer.
Students and young professionals who want flexible terms.
Those who prefer services and a single monthly price to managing a household.
People who do not want to attend house meetings or share decisions.
watchPoints: The company sets the rules and the price, and residents have little formal say.
Community depends on the operator's budget and can fade if it is cut.
Rooms are often small and the price can be higher than a regular rental.
Operators can fail or sell buildings, which can force residents to move.
flags: Habyt: 'absorbed Common and others' comes from the brief; central platform and 'sets terms centrally' are inferred, not checked.

The Collective: 2021 administration confirmed by The Collective's own FAQ and press; room count varies by source (546, 550, 551); a 2016 opening is confirmed. What happened to the building after the failure is unclear (Henderson Park sale, management buyout reported), so the leaving example says only that it was left to be sold and run by others.
The Collective private studios and lounges: described from general knowledge of the scheme, not checked.
Cohabs: 'host for each location' is assumed from the 'house by house' brief and not checked.
Campus1 MTL: only the brief's description (purpose-built student coliving downtown Montréal) is used.
Contract lengths, staff entry notices and app features are general patterns across operators, not tied to a named operator.
